lastText: File ClosedThe Road Not Taken to AthensContestedSoviet High Command, 1939–1945End of hostilities: MARCH 1945 (PROJECTED)Immediate AftermathVictory in Europe arrives around March 1945: earlier than the historical May 1945, bought with a faster, costlier advance. The army that reaches Berlin has paid for the ground twice over: a war fought closer to the historical pattern of holding rigid lines regardless of the arithmetic, at the cost this campaign keeps returning to. The industrial evacuation was subordinated to front supply in 1941: easing that autumn's crisis at a cost in Urals production capacity that every later year of this campaign quietly pays for. The tank armies waited for the three fronts to close together and entered Prague on May 11, two days later than they did in the real war. The Seelow Heights fell on the second day instead of the third, at a lower cost: the best the plan could have done, and not what happened. Berlin's fall was a certainty from the day the front stopped moving west; everything this campaign tracked was the cost of the miles back.One Year LaterVictory arrived ahead of the historical May 1945, which means the occupation of eastern and central Europe has had that much longer to harden by the time this account picks back up a year later. Within the year, the governments this front's advance put in place across Eastern Europe are consolidating along lines this campaign's own choices shaped only at the margins: the deeper political outcome was set
